Stamm · The R Statistical Language · Session 2 --- # Welcome back ## Where we left off {.inv} In Session 1 you built the core structures of R: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - the [console]{.green}, scripts, and R as a [calculator]{.green}; - [vectors]{.green}: the workhorse, and the four ways to subset them; - [lists]{.amber}: containers of anything, reached with `[[`/`$`; - [data frames]{.indigo} & [tibbles]{.indigo}: the tables you analyse; - [reading]{.indigo} & writing data files. ::: ## Today's map {.inv} ::: {.session-arc}
1Foundations
2Explore your data
3Repeat & package
::: Session 2 is the **"explore your data"** move of the course: take rows and columns you *stored*, and turn them into understanding. - [shape it]{.green}: the pipe `|>` and `dplyr`/`tidyr`: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`/`summarise`, `pivot_*`; - [read it]{.amber}: base-R workhorses, then [ggplot2]{.amber}'s layered grammar: histograms, scatters, facets, boxplots; - [understand it]{.indigo}: the **transform → plot → interpret** loop that is Exploratory Data Analysis. ::: {.callout-desc} **The thread.** We keep the penguins data the whole session: shape it, then plot it, then read the answers back off the plots. The EDA pipeline you build here is what the *repeat & package* session and the Reproducible Workflows course will build on. ::: # Tidyverse data transformation ## The tidyverse at a glance {.inv} A **family of R packages** that work as one: consistent syntax, a shared pipe, and the same *data frame in → data frame out* flow. - [readr]{.green}: bring data *in* (`read_csv`); - [tibble]{.green}: the modern data frame; - [dplyr]{.amber}: *transform* rows, columns, groups; - [tidyr]{.amber}: *reshape*: keep data [tidy]{.amber} (`pivot_*`); - [ggplot2]{.indigo}: *visualise*; - type-focused: `purrr` (iterate), `stringr` (strings), `forcats` (factors), `lubridate` (dates). ::: {.callout-desc} **Today we master `dplyr` + `tidyr`**: the transform engine that feeds every `ggplot` and every analysis. The long tail (`purrr`, `stringr`, …) you pick up on demand. ::: ## The pipe: `|>` {.inv} The pipe `|>` sends the value on its left into the *first argument* of the function on its right: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The pipe: top-to-bottom ```r penguins |> # raw data set dplyr::filter(species == "Adelie") |> # keep only Adelie penguins dplyr::mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) # compute a new column ``` ::: Reads: penguins, THEN filter(...). One line per data processing step: easy to comment/read. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The nested equivalent: inside-out ```r filtered_penguins <- dplyr::filter(penguins, species == "Adelie") dplyr::mutate(filtered_penguins, body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} The pipe keeps your script readable **top-to-bottom**; the nested alternative reads inside-out. The backbone of data work: one rule, **the data always goes first**. ::: ## Rows and columns: `filter` & `select` {.inv} Two verbs get you the *slice* you need: **rows** by a condition, **columns** by name: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} filter rows, select columns ```r penguins |> dplyr::filter(body_mass_g >= 4000) # keep rows that match penguins |> dplyr::filter(species != "Chinstrap", !is.na(sex)) # conditions AND together penguins |> dplyr::select(species, island, body_mass_g) # keep these columns penguins |> dplyr::select(-bill_depth_mm) # or drop just one ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} - `filter()` keeps **rows**; - `select()` keeps **columns**; - Multiple conditions in `filter` are AND-ed by default. ::: - Helper functions for `select()`: - Helper functions for `filter()`: ## New columns: `mutate` {.inv} `mutate()` computes **new columns** from existing ones, keeping everything else: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Compute a new column with `mutate()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::mutate(bmi = body_mass_g / (flipper_length_mm / 100)^2) |> dplyr::select(species, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, bmi) |> dplyr::slice(1:5) # show first 5 rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 4 species flipper_length_mm body_mass_g bmi 1 Adelie 181 3750 1145. 2 Adelie 186 3800 1098. 3 Adelie 195 3250 855. 4 Adelie NA NA NA 5 Adelie 193 3450 926. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - New columns are available to later steps in the **same** pipe; - You can `mutate()` several columns at once. ::: Helper functions for `mutate()`: ## Recode with `case_when` {.inv} `case_when()` turns a sequence of **if…else** conditions into a new column: a tidyverse-friendly replacement for nested `ifelse`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Multiple conditions, first match wins ```r penguins |> dplyr::mutate(size = dplyr::case_when( body_mass_g >= 5000 ~ "large", body_mass_g >= 3500 ~ "medium", .default = "small" )) ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} - `case_when` reads like a **look-up table**: each `condition ~ value` row is evaluated in order, and `.default` catches everything else; - Perfect for binning or relabelling inside a `mutate()`. ::: Documentation: ## Strings with `stringr` {.inv} `stringr` gives you one consistent family for **text**: every function is `str_*` with the string first, so they all pipe: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The `str_*` verbs: detect, replace, extract ```r penguins |> dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(species, "inst")) # species contains "inst" (Chinstrap…) species_clean <- penguins |> dplyr::mutate(species = stringr::str_to_title(species)) # "adelie" → "Adelie" ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} - `str_detect` pairs with `filter`, - `str_replace`/`str_to_*` with `mutate`: strings behave exactly like any tidyverse column once you use `str_*`. ::: Documentation: ## Sort: `arrange` {.inv} `arrange()` sorts the rows; wrap a column in `desc()` to go **descending**: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Ascending order ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Sort with `arrange()` / `desc()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::arrange(body_mass_g) # lightest first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Chinstrap Dream 46.9 16.6 192 2700 2 Adelie Biscoe 36.5 16.6 181 2850 3 Adelie Biscoe 36.4 17.1 184 2850 4 Adelie Biscoe 34.5 18.1 187 2900 5 Adelie Dream 33.1 16.1 178 2900 6 Adelie Torgers… 38.6 17 188 2900 7 Chinstrap Dream 43.2 16.6 187 2900 8 Adelie Biscoe 37.9 18.6 193 2925 9 Adelie Dream 37.5 18.9 179 2975 10 Adelie Dream 37 16.9 185 3000 # ℹ 334 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Descending order ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Sort with `arrange()` / `desc()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(body_mass_g), species) # heaviest first, ties by species ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g 1 Gentoo Biscoe 49.2 15.2 221 6300 2 Gentoo Biscoe 59.6 17 230 6050 3 Gentoo Biscoe 51.1 16.3 220 6000 4 Gentoo Biscoe 48.8 16.2 222 6000 5 Gentoo Biscoe 45.2 16.4 223 5950 6 Gentoo Biscoe 49.8 15.9 229 5950 7 Gentoo Biscoe 48.4 14.6 213 5850 8 Gentoo Biscoe 49.3 15.7 217 5850 9 Gentoo Biscoe 55.1 16 230 5850 10 Gentoo Biscoe 49.5 16.2 229 5800 # ℹ 334 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: sex , year ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Summarise by group {.inv} `group_by()` + `summarise()` collapse rows into **one row per group**: `group_by` sets the split, `summarise` reduces each group: ::: {.split-2}

::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `group_by()` + `summarise()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarise( n = dplyr::n(), avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 species n avg_mass 1 Adelie 152 3701. 2 Chinstrap 68 3733. 3 Gentoo 124 5076. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `n()` counts rows per group; `na.rm = TRUE` skips missing values. ::: ## `across()`: apply to many columns {.inv} `across()` applies one expression to **every column that matches** a selector: no copy-pasting verbs per column: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} Apply `mean` within a group, over several columns ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across( dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) )) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 6 species bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g year 1 Adelie 38.8 18.3 190. 3701. 2008. 2 Chinstrap 48.8 18.4 196. 3733. 2008. 3 Gentoo 47.5 15.0 217. 5076. 2008. ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} `across(where(is.numeric), …)` targets a whole **family** of columns at once: the bridge from "many similar lines" to programmatic thinking you'll meet again in Session 3's functions. ::: ## Reshape with [{tidyr}](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org): `pivot_longer` & `pivot_wider` {.inv} [Tidy data]{.amber}: one row per observation, one column per variable. Lab 1: tidyverse (≈25 min). Continue in lab-1-tidyverse.R. This is the foundation: the next lab (ggplot2) and the EDA in the Reproducible Workflows course build directly on it. Labs 1–2 together are the EDA half of the pipeline: transform in lab-1, plot in lab-2.

# Plotting with base R ## Why plot? {.inv} A plot is the fastest way to *feel* your data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic proof: four data sets with nearly identical means, variances and correlations, yet plots that look nothing alike. ::: {.split-2} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/anscombe-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: The four data sets share the same slope, intercept, correlation and means; only the *plots* tell them apart. A table could not, a `hist()` of a single column would not, an illustration does. ::: {.callout-desc} **The lesson.** Look at your data before you summarise it: a single well-chosen plot often tells you more than ten summary statistics. This is the heart of *Exploratory Data Analysis*. ::: ::: ## Histograms in base R {.inv} The simplest first look at one variable: **`hist()`**. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} A histogram of one variable ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure: dark slide would hide the default black ink hist( penguins$body_mass_g, # the variable breaks = 30, # how many bins col = "steelblue", border = "white", main = "Penguin body mass (g)" # title ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Positron draws the plot in the **Plots** pane. `hist()` is one call, but its defaults are utilitarian. ::: ## Other base-R workhorses {.inv} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Scatterplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide x <- rnorm(10) y <- rnorm(10) plot(x, y) # scatter plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Barplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide g <- rpois(n = 10L, lambda = 1) barplot(table(g)) # counts of categories ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Boxplot ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide boxplot(y ~ g) # one box per group ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ### Function plotting ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The rest of the base-R drawer ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} par(bg = "white") # opaque white figure so the default black ink shows on the dark slide curve(sin, 0, 2*pi) # plot a function ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} Base R can already do a lot, but its look is dated and customisation is verbose: *why* we meet **ggplot2** next. ::: ## The limit of base-R plots {.inv} Base `plot()` is fine for a quick peek. For **publication-grade** graphics (faceting, legends, themes, layered encodings), it gets unwieldy fast. That's the gap **ggplot2** fills: a single coherent *grammar*, rather than a grab-bag of functions. ::: {.callout-desc} You'll implement several of these base-R plots **by hand in lab 2**, then rebuild one in ggplot2 to feel the difference. ::: # ggplot2 ## The grammar of graphics {.inv} **ggplot2** (part of the tidyverse) builds every plot from a few composable pieces: ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} - **[data]{.green}**: a data frame (usually a tibble); - **[aesthetics]{.green}** (`aes`): *which variables* map to *which visual channel* (x, y, colour, size, fill, …); - **[geometries]{.amber}** (`geom_*`): *how* the data are drawn (points, lines, bars, histograms, …); - **[facets]{.indigo}**: small multiples, splitting by a variable; - **[scales/themes]{.indigo}**: the polish. ::: ## The first ggplot {.inv} Every plot starts with `ggplot(data, aes(...))`, then adds layers with `+`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} The first ggplot ```r ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} This is the *same histogram* we drew in base R, but now each piece is explicit and easy to extend. ::: ## Scatter: two continuous variables {.inv} Mapping variables to `x` and `y`, and a third to `color`: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
                      y = body_mass_g))
  + geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.7)
  + theme_dark()
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.callout-desc} **Read it aloud.** "Body mass grows with flipper length", and each species clusters in its own region of this space. That's a finding you'd never see from `summary()`. ::: ::: ## One variable per facet {.inv} **Faceting** splits the plot into small multiples: one per level of a variable: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g))
  + geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#2E7D6B",
                    color = "#17251F")
  + facet_wrap(~ species, ncol = 1)
  + theme_dark()
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.callout-desc} Different species have *different* distributions of body mass: a comparison that's hard to see in one pooled histogram. ::: ::: ## Boxplots for groups {.inv} Categorical `x` + continuous `y`: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g,
                      fill = species))
  + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8)
  + theme_dark()
  + theme(legend.position = "none")
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.callout-desc} A boxplot shows the median, the box (IQR) and outliers at a glance: ideal for comparing a numeric variable *across groups*. ::: ::: ## Order factors with `forcats` {.inv} Plots order themselves however the factor levels say: `forcats` (part of the tidyverse) lets you **reorder** those levels so graphs tell the story you want: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%"} `fct_reorder` sorts a factor by another variable ```r penguins |> mutate(species = fct_reorder(species, body_mass_g, median, na.rm = TRUE)) |> ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} `fct_reorder` puts the *highest median first* on the axis: order becomes part of your message. `fct_relevel`/`fct_lump` fine-tune and collapse rare levels. ::: ## Layers compose {.inv} An important ggplot2 habit: plots are built from **many layers**. For example, scatter + a smooth trend: ::: {.split-2} 
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
                      y = body_mass_g))
  + geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.6)
  + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
                 color = "#E8A33D", linewidth = 1)
  + theme_dark()
::: {.plot-stack} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="1"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="2"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="3"} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-2_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=624 class="fragment step-plot" data-fragment-index="4"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.callout-desc} `geom_point()` and `geom_smooth()` *layer* on the same plot, each with its own mapping. This layering is what makes ggplot2 so expressive. ::: ::: ## A grammar, not a menu {.inv} The power is **consistency**: you learn a few verbs (`geom_point`, `geom_bar`, `geom_histogram`, `facet_wrap`, `aes`) and combine them, instead of memorising a different function per plot type. There's a gallery of extensions (e.g. `{ggpubr}`, `{patchwork}`, `{plotly}` for interactivity). ::: {.callout-desc} We'll run a *ggplot2 build-up* live: from a bare histogram to a faceted, titled, themed figure in a handful of added lines. Watch how small edits compound. ::: ## Your turn: plotting {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. Load penguins with `read_csv("penguins.csv")`. 2. Base R: scatter `body_mass_g` vs `flipper_length_mm`, by species. 3. ggplot2: same plot with `color = species`. 4. `hist()` of `body_mass_g` + `facet_wrap(~ species)`. 5. Which approach would you reach for? :::
Lab 2: plotting

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
